content: 1. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the relationship between sedentary behavior (SB) and bone health in children, adolescents, and young adults (up to 24 years old). Seventeen observational studies were included, and data were extracted and analyzed independently by two reviewers. This association was independent of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA). However, there was insufficient evidence to link SB with lumbar spine bone outcomes, and no association was observed between SB and total body bone outcomes in high-quality studies using DXA. 2. A systematic review examined the influence of physical activity (PA) and sports on bone geometry in children and adolescents. Twenty-one studies were included, and most reported that PA and sports positively impacted bone geometry and bone mineral density. Sports such as gymnastics, soccer, and other weight-bearing activities were associated with better bone geometry outcomes compared to non-weight-bearing activities like swimming. The findings suggest that frequent and intense weight-bearing sports are beneficial for bone health. 3. A systematic review investigated the role of youth sports participation in promoting physical activity and preventing pediatric obesity in children aged 6 to 19 years. Of the 27 included studies, 15 demonstrated that greater engagement in organized youth sports was associated with higher levels of physical activity during adolescence and later life. However, evidence linking youth sports participation to obesity-related outcomes, such as BMI and body fat percentage, was inconsistent. 4. A meta-analysis explored the relationship between sedentary video gaming and body mass. Based on 20 studies involving 38,097 participants, the results showed a small and inconsistent association between sedentary video gaming and body mass, primarily observed in adults. There was little evidence to support the idea that video gaming displaces physical activity. The findings challenge the assumption of a strong link between sedentary gaming and obesity. 5. A systematic review examined the association between physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and academic achievement in children and adolescents aged 6 to 18 years. However, self-reported physical activity and cardiorespiratory fitness were generally positively associated with academic performance. Physical activity did not negatively impact academic outcomes. 6. A systematic review assessed the effects of classroom-based physical activity interventions on physical activity levels, learning outcomes, and health in school-aged children. Fifteen studies were included, and interventions integrating physical activity with academic content were found to increase physical activity levels and improve learning outcomes. Teachers and students responded positively to these programs, which also showed benefits for BMI and on-task behavior. 7. A systematic review evaluated the association between pedometer-determined physical activity and adiposity in children and adolescents. Thirty-six studies were included, with consistent evidence showing that higher levels of walking were protective against obesity. However, more longitudinal studies are needed to establish dose-response relationships and to focus on younger children. 8. A systematic review examined the relationship between physical activity, diet, and cardiometabolic health in Malaysian adolescents. Seventeen studies were included, but all were of poor quality. Evidence for associations between physical activity and cardiometabolic health indicators, such as BMI and body fat percentage, was weak and inconsistent. 9. A meta-analysis synthesized evidence on the effectiveness of school-based physical activity interventions on cardiometabolic risk factors in children. Nineteen randomized controlled trials involving 11,988 children aged 3 to 12 years were included. However, implementation details and compliance rates were often lacking in the studies. 10. A systematic review summarized the effects of physical activity interventions on cognitive and academic performance in children. Of the 58 included studies, 11 were rated as high quality. Beneficial effects of physical activity on cognitive performance were observed in 48% of constructs analyzed, while 60% of analyses found positive effects on academic performance. Strong evidence supported the benefits of physical activity on mathematics performance. The review emphasized the need for high-quality research to clarify the causal relationship between physical activity and cognitive/academic outcomes. 11. The findings highlighted the importance of reducing sedentary time and increasing physical activity to improve cardiometabolic health outcomes.
